rationale: The answer covers each required mechanism. (1) It says an illiquid or wide underlying basket raises hedging risk and leads market makers to quote wider. Hedging costs (basket or futures execution plus inventory risk) and creation/redemption costs (fees, taxes, basket sourcing) widen the arbitrage band and therefore the quote. This matches the cost-pass-through logic, though it never explicitly says market makers earn the spread. (2) It says historical volume reflects only secondary-market trading and misses creation/redemption capacity, underlying depth and stress behaviour. That captures why share volume alone is incomplete, though it does not say directly that creation/redemption lets market makers adjust inventory beyond existing ETF shares. It gives no universal spread levels and promises no capacity. The closing line favours underlying conditions and creation/redemption capacity over trading activity, which comes close to ranking but is a reasonable framing. One localized slip: 'trades in hours when the ETF does' should say 'does not', but the intended timing-mismatch driver is clear and is an allowed extra driver. No material error in the central content.
